<reason>B won the interpretive battle over Karikó—reframing A's marquee example as evidence for portability (she survived because money existed outside her institution's control)—and A's "many doors, one gatekeeper" counter was answered a level deeper: appeal among fallible judges beats one final judge, and under block funding the wrong no is the last word. B's Rebuttal 2 caught a real contradiction (A called competition "perpetual boom-bust" yet claimed it "never closed anything") and deflated A's one concrete closure example (Mill Hill) as relocation, not exit. A argued well—strong selection-effects case, the lottery-obituary jab, the accountability-reversal—but B's "what happens after a judge is wrong" frame subsumed A's best points, and B's closing turned A's own line ("a default cannot tell a dead lab from a daring one") into the decisive concession: "Neither can a director." Both sides were disciplined and well-grounded; B simply drove the comparison to a cleaner resolution.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 8): exposed A's internal contradiction (boom-bust vs. "never closed anything"), reduced Mill Hill to "money changed postcode," and crystallized the asymmetry-of-default frame that decided the debate—sealed by B's closing reversal of A's own default line.</best_rebuttal>
